doc.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: The banjo, rhythm and the New Orleans style
title: Watching the town's banjo players and sitting in at the Alley Club
summary: After the juke box thinned out work, Barker watched Johnny Davis, Son Thomas, the Marreros and others, and filled in for Caffrey Darensbourg at a downtown club.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: What was the next step for you in music after the Boozan Kings?

You’re around there. You see bands, so you’re going to decide whether you’re going to play music for a living or you’re going to cop out and do it pasttime. But it’s kind of rough playing, always was playing music for a living in New Orleans, because there’s so many musicians and so many clubs. And then the juke box came in, and that killed off a lot of work. Man don’t need you only if he got Louis Armstrong on the juke box.
What was your next musical group after the Boozan Kings?

I left that as kids. I started playing professional, rehearsing with different musicians around town. Little small musicians, but I’m listening to bigtimers and watching what they’re doing. Everywhere Kid Rena played, sometimes Buddy Petit, Sam Morgan, I went by and watched the banjo player all night.
Who were some of those banjo players that you listened to?
Johnny Dave [Davis] was with Sam Morgan.
Johnny Dave you were listening to?

Johnny Dave. Son Thomas was with Kid Rena. MacLean, Richard MacLean, great banjo player. George Guesnon. John Marrerro. Lawrence Marrerro. Caffrey Darensbourg was working the Alley Club downtown, and he . . . I’d go to the club, and he’d see me out front by the bar. I was on long pants then, and he’d say, “Want to play a little while for me, man? Lay something on.” I’d say, “Yeah.” So I’d go back. The band relished me, because I think I had a little more spark than he had. Then I was trying to impress them too. Playing. Trying to jazz up the band. That’s what I do now. I put that figure-eight stroke on them bands. I rigamarolle like I did on that record, and that spices up the bands.
